newsitem.title: UK: Looming election heats up risk for Japanese bonds.
newsitem.headline: Looming election heats up risk for Japanese bonds.

text.p: Political uncertainty ahead of Japan's general elections on October 20 will keep overseas investors out of Japanese government bonds despite the recent rally, analysts said on Tuesday.
Even once the election has passed, rate hike speculation will prevent funds from moving into JGBs, they said.

"Political agitation going into the election is leading to a lot of rate and currency statements," said Sean Shepley, international economist at CS First Boston in London. "As that has risen, the surge of interest in JGBs has died away."
The election for the 500-seat Lower House is the first since July 1993.
Since it was called in September, markets have been buzzing with speculation over when rock-bottom interest rates would rise amid reports of statements from senior government officials.

On Tuesday, JGBs rallied after a newswire reported that Eisukie Sakakibara, director general of the Japanese Finance Ministry's international bureau, said rates were unlikely to be raised until at least the end of the fiscal year to March 31.
Sakakibara later denied the comments and JGBs retreated.
Japan's official discount rate (ODR) is at 0.50 percent.

"We are particularly wary of the short end, and consider the five- to ten-year area much safer," said Peter Frank, senior economist at Sumitomo Finance International in London. "But right now the ten-year area is so expensive, nowhere is safe."
Shepley said foreign investors were worried that unhedged JGB positions were vulnerable to currency risks and were likely to remain underweight of the market.
Analysts said beyond the election, the main uncertainty was the rate outlook for Japan.
The market is still on the lookout for a 25 basis point hike in the ODR although speculation about the timing varies.
Frank said the recent rally left the market expensive but there was no sign of a trigger for prices to push lower.
December JGB futures in Tokyo set a contract high of 122.60 on September 26, after ralling from a low of 116.75 on July 17. Yield on the benchmark 182nd 10-year JGB stood at 2.820 percent.
On a spread basis, Shepley said he expected some outperformance by JGBs over U.S. Treasuries as U.S. bonds continued to suffer from interest rate anxiety.
Peter Wilson, strategist at Tokyo Mitsubishi in London, said the market could push higher, despite the recent rally.
"The upward price action is very strong and any dips immediately bore the market," he said.
Japan auctioned 500 billon yen ($4.50 billion) worth of 1.7 percent four-year government notes.
Wilson said he advised British funds to hold some JGBs, but to hedge the currency risk. "Hedged JGBs are dollar currency risk," he said. "There is no exposure to yen weakness." ($1=111.1 Yen)
